script: [serious] Apollo 13 was in trouble before it ever left the ground. The oxygen tank that exploded had been damaged on Earth, twice, and nobody caught it. In 1968, at the factory, the shelf holding that tank was accidentally dropped about two inches. Engineers decided it was probably fine. Years earlier, the tank's heaters had been redesigned to handle sixty-five volts on the launch pad, not just the spacecraft's twenty-eight. Every part was upgraded except one. The tiny safety switches that cut the heater off. Two weeks before launch, the tank wouldn't drain during a test. So technicians ran its heater for hours to boil the oxygen off. The safety switches welded shut. The heat inside likely passed a thousand degrees, and burned the insulation off the wires. But the gauge only read up to eighty degrees, so nobody knew. April 13th, 1970. Two hundred thousand miles from Earth, the crew switched on the fans in that tank. A spark. An explosion. Houston, we've had a problem. Jim Lovell, Fred Haise and Jack Swigert used their lunar module as a lifeboat, and made it home. Send this to someone who thinks one tiny part can't matter. This is Dossier Decoded. Case file number forty-eight. A new file every day.
